name: Password storage and authentication-scheme analysis
theory_paragraphs: The threat model is the \term{offline attack}: the attacker (Mallory) has stolen a copy of the password database and computes hashes at her own pace -- rate limiting and lockouts do not apply. Passwords must never be stored in plaintext; instead the server stores $uid, H(p)$ where $H$ is a \term{secure cryptographic hash function}: \imp{deterministic, one-way, and collision resistant}. \term{One-wayness} (preimage resistance) is the load-bearing property here: given a stored digest, Mallory cannot invert it, so her only option is to GUESS candidate passwords, hash them, and compare. Since users pick passwords from a small effective list of $L$ candidates (the top-20 passwords alone cover roughly 10\% of accounts), this \term{dictionary attack} is devastatingly practical. Precomputed digest lists (\term{rainbow tables}) make it a pure lookup.

The defense is a \term{salt}: a per-user, random, PUBLIC value stored alongside the digest, so the server stores $uid, s, H(s \,\|\, p)$. The salt does not need to be secret -- its job is to make each user's digest function different, which destroys cross-user reuse of precomputation. The cost asymmetry to memorize: with $U$ users and a candidate list of size $L$, unsalted cracking costs about $L + U$ work (hash the list once, compare everywhere -- $O(L+U)$), while per-user-salted cracking costs $U \cdot L$ (re-hash the whole list per user -- $O(U \cdot L)$). Two further refinements: a \term{slow hash / KDF} (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2 iterating HMAC tens of thousands of times) multiplies every guess by a large constant factor that a user barely notices but an attacker hashing billions of guesses cannot afford; and \imp{a single global salt is not a salt} -- it leaves all users sharing one digest function, so rainbow tables work again.

In the exam's cost-accounting model \imp{only hash evaluations count}: comparisons, concatenations, and database reads/writes are free. Every sub-question is then pure arithmetic driven by one principle -- \term{factor the stored-value formula} into \begin{tightitem}\item \term{user-independent subexpressions} (anything built only from the password, e.g. $H(p)$): precompute once for all $L$ candidates and reuse across users;\item \term{per-user subexpressions} (anything the username or salt touches, e.g. $H(user \,\|\, p)$ or $H(user)$): must be recomputed per user.\end{tightitem}The placement of $H$ decides everything: $H(p)$ as an INNER term is reusable (dictionary of size $L$), while $H$ wrapped AROUND the username forces $U \cdot L$ fresh evaluations.

\term{Lamport hash chains} (one-time passwords) appear as the second scheme family. At registration the client computes a chain $H^{N}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ (apply $H$ a total of $N$ times) and the server stores it in a variable \term{stored}. At login number $i$ the client sends $H^{N-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$; the server verifies $H(\text{received}) = stored$ and, on success, updates $stored := \text{received}$. Consequences of one-wayness: \begin{tightitem}\item the server needs to know NEITHER $pwd$ NOR $salt$ -- it only ever hashes the received token and compares;\item the next token $H^{N-i-1}$ cannot be derived from the current one (that would invert $H$), so the client recomputes it from $pwd \,\|\, salt$ at cost $N-i-1$ hashes;\item at login $i = N$ the client sends $H^{0}(pwd \,\|\, salt) = pwd \,\|\, salt$ in plaintext -- an eavesdropper then learns everything;\item an attacker who can WRITE $stored$ picks any value $v$, sets $stored := H(v)$, and logs in by sending $v$.\end{tightitem}
theory_cheatsheet: Cost model: only hash evaluations count; comparisons and DB operations are free.
Unsalted $H(p)$: recover all $U$ passwords costs $L$ hashes; set all to a new password costs $1$ hash.
Username/salt inside the OUTER hash kills reuse: recovery $U \cdot L$, replacement $U$.
$H(pwd)$ as an INNER term: precompute the dictionary once: recovery $L + U \cdot L$; replacement $1 + U$ (the new password is NOT in the list, so its inner hash costs 1 extra).
$H(user)$ as an inner term: precomputable once per user, adding a flat $+U$ term.

Lamport chain: login $i$ sends $H^{N-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$; server checks $H(\text{received}) = stored$; next token cannot be derived from the current (one-wayness); login $N$ leaks $pwd$ in plaintext; DB-writer sets $stored := H(v)$ and logs in with $v$.
identify_givens: A password database with $U$ users whose passwords come from a known list of $L$ candidates, a concrete storage formula built from a secure hash $H$ and concatenation (e.g. $H(password)$, $H(username \,\|\, password)$, $H(H(username) \,\|\, password)$, $H(username \,\|\, H(password))$), and an attacker Mallory who can read and modify the database; or a Lamport-style hash-chain scheme using $H^{k}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ with a server-side \q{stored} variable and a network- or server-compromising attacker. Only hash computations count as cost; comparisons and database operations are free.
identify_target: For each storage scheme, describe the attack and compute the exact number of hash evaluations needed (a) to recover every user's password and (b) to change every password to a fixed new value such as \q{pwned}; or, for hash-chain schemes, justify what the server must know, compute the chain index/cost of the next login, state at which login an eavesdropper learns the password, and show how a server-compromising attacker logs in without $pwd$, $salt$, or the login index.

algorithm.detail: Write down the exact stored-value formula, the attacker's capabilities (read DB, modify DB, eavesdrop logins, compromise server), and the goal:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{recovery}: determine every user's password;\item \term{replacement}: overwrite all entries so every password becomes a fixed new value (e.g. pwned).\end{tightitem}Recall the cost model: \imp{only hash evaluations count}.

Split the hash expression into\begin{tightitem}\item \term{user-independent subexpressions} -- precompute once, reuse for all users. E.g. $H(password)$ is the same for every user: a dictionary of all $L$ values costs $L$ hashes total.\item \term{per-user subexpressions} -- anything concatenated with the username or a per-user salt must be recomputed for each user.\end{tightitem}This factoring decides the entire answer.

For each of the $U$ users, test all $L$ candidates against the stored value; total = (one-time precomputation) $+\; U \times L \times$ (hashes per candidate after reuse). The four canonical shapes:\begin{tightitem}\item $H(pwd)$: $L$ (one dictionary serves all users).\item $H(user \,\|\, pwd)$: $U \cdot L$ (salt kills reuse).\item $H(H(user) \,\|\, pwd)$: $U + U \cdot L$ (precompute $H(user)$ per user).\item $H(user \,\|\, H(pwd))$: $L + U \cdot L$ (precompute the $L$ hashed passwords).\end{tightitem}

Apply the same factoring to the new password pwned: compute its user-independent inner hash once if the formula needs it, then one outer hash per user:\begin{tightitem}\item $H(pwned)$: $1$ hash, written everywhere.\item $H(user \,\|\, pwned)$: $U$ hashes.\item $H(H(user) \,\|\, pwned)$: $U + U = 2U$.\item $H(user \,\|\, H(pwned))$: $1 + U$.\end{tightitem}Trap: \imp{pwned is not in the candidate list}, so its inner hash can never come from the dictionary precomputation -- it costs one extra evaluation.

If a goal requires inverting $H$ (recovering a password outside the candidate list, or walking a hash chain backwards), state that it is \term{infeasible because $H$ is one-way}. Likewise state that the server only needs to know the values it actually compares -- it never needs $pwd$ or $salt$ themselves.

For Lamport-style schemes where login $i$ sends $H^{N-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ and the server checks $H(\text{received}) = stored$ then updates $stored$:\begin{tightitem}\item The next login needs exponent $N-i-1$; it CANNOT be derived from the sent value (one-wayness) and costs full recomputation from $pwd \,\|\, salt$, i.e. $N-i-1$ hashes.\item At login $N$ the client sends $H^{0}(pwd \,\|\, salt) = pwd \,\|\, salt$ in plaintext -- an eavesdropper learns the password here.\item An attacker who can write $stored$ sets $stored := H(v)$ for a chosen $v$ and logs in with $v$ -- no knowledge of $pwd$, $salt$, or $i$ required.\end{tightitem}

Give the final count per scheme and per goal as a closed formula in $U$ and $L$ (e.g. $L$ and $1$; $U \cdot L$ and $U$; $U + U \cdot L$ and $2U$; $L + U \cdot L$ and $U + 1$), each with one line of justification naming what was precomputed and what is per-user.

variations.name: Hash placement / nesting
variations.detail: The professor permutes where $H$ and the username sit: $H(password)$, $H(username \,\|\, password)$, $H(H(username) \,\|\, password)$, $H(username \,\|\, H(password))$. Where the inner hash sits decides what is reusable: a dictionary of $H(pwd)$ is reusable across users only when $H(pwd)$ appears as an INNER term (giving $L + U \cdot L$ instead of $U \cdot L$); $H(username)$ is precomputable once per user (adding a flat $U$). Trap: forgetting that pwned is not in the $L$-list, so its inner hash costs one extra evaluation in the replacement attack ($U + 1$, not $U$).

variations.name: Lamport hash-chain login
variations.detail: Instead of a static database, the scheme sends $H^{N-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ at login $i$ and the server verifies $H(\text{received}) = stored$. Sub-questions ask whether the server needs $pwd$/$salt$ (no -- it only compares hashes), the cost of the next login (full recomputation; the chain cannot be walked backwards), when an eavesdropper learns $pwd$ (at $i = N$, since $H^{0}(x) = x$ is sent in plaintext), and the server-compromise attack (set $stored := H(v)$, log in with $v$). Trap: thinking the next token can be derived from the current one -- one-wayness forbids it.

variations.name: Role reversal: attacker writes the database
variations.detail: The second goal always flips the attacker from reader to writer: instead of cracking, Mallory replaces stored hashes so every user has password pwned. The cost structure mirrors recovery but with $L$ replaced by the single value pwned. Traps: reusing the dictionary of $L$ password hashes for pwned (impossible -- pwned is not in the list), or forgetting that the per-user salt forces $U$ separate outer hashes.

variations.name: Design-critique checklist
variations.detail: Other sittings list organizational measures (secret proprietary hash, one global \q{salt}, strict composition rules, forced rotation, lockout, phone recovery) and ask which attack each counters. Map each measure: a proprietary hash violates \term{Kerckhoffs' principle}; a global salt is not a salt and does not stop rainbow tables -- only per-user salts do; lockout/rate limiting stops ONLINE guessing but enables user-targeted DoS; a \term{slow KDF} (bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2/PBKDF2) raises OFFLINE cracking cost. Adapt by naming the attack each measure does and does not address.

original_steps.work: Goals: (1) recover all $U$ passwords; (2) overwrite all stored digests so every password becomes letmein. Only hash evaluations count; comparisons, concatenations, and DB writes are free. For the prototype login, Trudy additionally eavesdrops the network (iii) and can write $stored$ (iv).

Factoring. In (a) and (c) the term $H(password)$ is user-independent, so one dictionary of all $L$ values of $H(candidate)$ is reusable across users. In (b), (c), and (d) the OUTER hash mixes in the username, forcing per-user recomputation. In (d) the inner $H(username)$ is constant per user and precomputable once per user. For the replacement attack, note that letmein is not in the candidate list, so $H(letmein)$ must be computed fresh (one extra hash) wherever an inner $H(pwd)$ is needed.

Recovery costs. (a) Hash each of the $L$ candidates once and compare the digests with all $U$ stored values: \[ L \text{ hashes.} \] (b) The username sits inside the outer hash, so no reuse: for each user, hash the whole list, $U \cdot L$ hashes. (c) Precompute the dictionary $H(candidate)$ for all $L$ candidates ($L$ hashes), then per user compute $H(H(candidate) \,\|\, username)$ for all $L$ candidates: \[ L + U \cdot L \text{ hashes.} \] (d) Precompute $H(username)$ once per user ($U$ hashes), then per user compute $H(candidate \,\|\, H(username))$ for all $L$ candidates: \[ U + U \cdot L \text{ hashes.} \]

Replacement costs (new password letmein). (a) Compute $H(letmein)$ once and write it into all $U$ entries: $1$ hash. (b) Per user compute $H(letmein \,\|\, username)$: $U$ hashes. (c) Compute $H(letmein)$ once (letmein is not in the list, so the dictionary does not help), then per user $H(H(letmein) \,\|\, username)$: \[ 1 + U \text{ hashes.} \] (d) Per user compute $H(username)$ ($U$ hashes, or reuse from the recovery phase -- counted fresh here), then per user $H(letmein \,\|\, H(username))$ ($U$ hashes): \[ 2U \text{ hashes.} \]

Impossibility notes. (i) The server needs NEITHER $pwd$ NOR $salt$: it only computes one hash of the received token and compares it with $stored$; the chain was created by the client at registration. (ii) First half: deriving the next token $H^{500-(i+1)}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ from the token $H^{500-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$ just sent would require inverting $H$ once -- infeasible because $H$ is one-way.

Hash-chain answers. (ii) At login $i+1$ the client must send $H^{499-i}(pwd \,\|\, salt)$; it cannot derive this from the login-$i$ token and must recompute from $pwd \,\|\, salt$, costing $499 - i$ hash evaluations. (iii) At login $i = 500$ the client sends $H^{0}(pwd \,\|\, salt) = pwd \,\|\, salt$ in plaintext, so an eavesdropper learns $pwd \,\|\, salt$ at the 500th login. (iv) Server-compromise attack: Trudy picks any value $v$ of her choice, overwrites $stored := H(v)$, and sends $v$ as the login token; the server computes $H(v)$, finds it equal to $stored$, accepts the login, and updates $stored := v$. No knowledge of $pwd$, $salt$, or $i$ is needed.

Totals. (a) $L$ and $1$; (b) $U \cdot L$ and $U$; (c) $L + U \cdot L$ and $U + 1$; (d) $U + U \cdot L$ and $2U$. Prototype: server stores only a digest (needs neither $pwd$ nor $salt$); login $i+1$ costs $499-i$ fresh hashes; $pwd \,\|\, salt$ leaks at login $500$; a DB-writing attacker logs in via $stored := H(v)$ with self-chosen $v$.
